title: The tree on the riverbank
hook: life is a tree on the riverbank; how long can it stand (Farid salok)

segments.voice: Yesterday, rukhi sukhi: eat what's in front of you, and don't long for another's buttered bread. Your line was dry bread is enough. How did your plain meal taste? Day seven hundred sixty-five.

Rivers in the Punjab move. In the rains they swell, and the water works at the banks all season, quietly carrying the soil away a little at a time. A tree growing right on the edge can look strong for years: thick trunk, wide shade, birds in it. But its roots are in earth the river is slowly taking. Farid looked at a tree like that and saw something about every life. Today: the tree on the riverbank.
screen: `THE RIVER WORKS AT THE BANK.` → `A STRONG TREE ON THE EDGE.` → `FARID SEES A LIFE.`

segments.voice: The couplet, on Ang 1382, in paraphrase: a little tree on the riverbank, how long can it hold firm? Farid, in an unbaked clay pot, how long can water be kept? Two pictures, the same question, and he doesn't answer it. He doesn't need to. Look at the first picture. Farid's word is rukhra, which some readers hear as the little tree, a tender word. He's not sneering at it, and the couplet says nothing against the tree. The trouble isn't in the tree. It's in where every tree stands, on ground that's being carried off. Then the second picture, from a potter's yard. A pot that hasn't been fired in the kiln looks like a pot. You can pour water into it. But the water starts softening the clay from the inside, and before long it seeps out, or the pot gives way. Farid sets the body there: a pot of soft clay, holding something for a while. Some hear this as gloomy. Read it next to his other saloks and it sounds more like a friend's warning. Farid keeps asking a practical question: since the bank won't hold forever, what will you do with the time? Earlier in these days he called himself to rise and pray before dawn; now we can hear why he didn't put it off. Sikhs hear the same note in the Gurus' teaching that a human life is a precious chance, not to be slept through. The tree on the edge isn't a reason for fear. It's a reason to stand well, today, while it stands.
screen: `HOW LONG CAN THE TREE HOLD FIRM?` · `RUKHRA — THE LITTLE TREE.` · `WATER IN AN UNBAKED POT.` · `NOT GLOOM: WHAT WILL YOU DO WITH THE TIME?` · then, large: `HOW LONG CAN IT STAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by water. If you can, stand near water now, a sink, a glass, a window with rain, a fountain, a river if you're lucky. If not, picture the riverbank. Stand, feet planted, like the tree. Feel your weight on the ground. Breathe. Let the question come, without any fear in it: while I'm standing, what's worth doing today? Wait for one plain answer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Rukhra. Farid's little tree on the riverbank: strong, giving shade, and standing on ground the river is slowly taking.
Your line: how long can it stand. Today, do the one thing your answer named, before the day carries it away. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of Gurbani; Sikhs hear in them the Gurus' own reminder that human life is short and precious, a chance to remember the Name.

fork.setup: you're a tree on the riverbank, strong and giving shade, and the river is slowly taking the bank. what does Farid's question point you toward?
options: pretend the bank will hold forever.
stand well and use the time while you stand.
fork.reveal: Farid asks how long the tree can hold firm, and read with his other saloks, it's a friend's warning: don't put off what matters.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the little tree on the riverbank in Farid's couplet.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy line about death.
what it means: a life is a strong tree on a bank the river is taking; so use the time while it stands.
what a scholar hears: Farid pairs it with water in an unbaked pot, and calls it rukhra, the little tree, with tenderness, not scorn.

sources.ref: Salok Sheikh Farid (kandhi utai rukhra), Ang 1382

notes: The index gives no Ang; 'kandhi utai rukhra kichrak bannai dheer; farida kachai bhaandai rakheeai kichar taaee neer' placed at Ang 1382 from memory. Please confirm Ang and paraphrase.
'rukhra' as a diminutive with tenderness ('the little tree'): confirm this reading; Gurmukhi spelling ਰੁਖੜਾ to confirm.
Hook's description of Punjab rivers eroding banks in the rains is general description, not a claim from the text; confirm it is acceptable.
Link to the Gurus' teaching that human life is a precious chance is general; a Keeper may wish to name a line.
Editor pass: cut 'Farid lived by a river, in a river town' (a biographical claim the salok doesn't make); the diminutive reading of rukhra is now framed as 'some readers hear'.

Audit pass: the teach and myth said the tree 'is doing everything right: growing, giving shade', which the couplet does not say; now 'the couplet says nothing against the tree'. The hook's strong, shady tree stays as a scene, not a claim about the text.
